title: Episode 214: France: Joan of Arc, the Voices of Domremy, and the Liberation of Orléans
description:
In the darkest hour of the Hundred Years' War, with northern France occupied by English armies and the Burgundian faction, the sovereign existence of France hung by a thread. The uncrowned Dauphin, Charles VII, was impoverished and dispirited, trapped south of the Loire River while the strategic gateway city of Orléans endured a suffocating English siege. Out of the humble eastern village of Domremy arose a seventeen-year-old illiterate peasant girl named Joan of Arc, who claimed that heavenly voices of Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret had commanded her to lift the siege of Orléans and crown the Dauphin at Reims. Donning white armor, cutting her hair, and carrying a holy white banner, Joan rallied the French soldiers with fiery spiritual resolve, breaking the English siege of Orléans in nine days and leading Charles to his sacred coronation. Betrayed, captured at Compiègne, and subjected to a corrupt ecclesiastical show trial, Joan died at the stake at nineteen, leaving behind an immortal legend as the patron saint and savior of France.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we begin our exploration of France with one of the most astonishing figures in world history: Joan of Arc. In an era when women held no military or political power, a teenage peasant girl transformed the destiny of a nation. Here is George with the story of the voices of Domremy, the white banner of Orléans, and the martyr's stake.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: A KINGDOM IN RUINS: THE HUNDRED YEARS' WAR
By the early fifteenth century, the Kingdom of France had been ravaged by nearly a century of intermittent, catastrophic warfare against the Kingdom of England, known as the Hundred Years' War. In 1415, King Henry V of England had shattered the French chivalric army at the Battle of Agincourt with his deadly longbowmen, conquering Normandy. In 1420, under the humiliating Treaty of Troyes, the insane French King Charles VI disinherited his own son, the Dauphin Charles, declaring Henry V the rightful heir to the French crown. When both kings died in 1422, the infant Henry VI of England was proclaimed King of England and France in Paris, supported by the powerful, treacherous Duke of Burgundy. The disinherited Dauphin Charles VII, mocked as the 'King of Bourges,' held precarious sway only over central and southern France. Impoverished, doubting his own legitimacy, and lacking military resolve, Charles watched in despair as English armies under the Duke of Bedford moved south to lay siege to Orléans in October 1428. If Orléans fell, the Loire River would be crossed, and France would cease to exist as an independent kingdom.  The desperate plight of France in 1428 was magnified by an ancient rural prophecy, attributed to Merlin, which whispered that France would be lost by a wicked woman—identified as Queen Isabeau of Bavaria who signed the Treaty of Troyes—and saved by a pure virgin from the oak forests of Lorraine.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE HEAVENLY VOICES OF DOMREMY
In the peaceful, rolling pastures of Domremy on the border of Lorraine, a peasant girl named Jeanne—known to history as Joan of Arc—was born around 1412. Uneducated and illiterate, Joan spent her childhood spinning wool and tending sheep, known by her neighbors for her extraordinary piety and devotion to church bells. Around the age of thirteen, while working in her father's garden at noon in summer, Joan saw a brilliant, blinding light and heard a supernatural voice. The Archangel Michael, accompanied by Saint Catherine of Alexandria and Saint Margaret of Antioch, appeared to her in bodily form, commanding her to live a pure life. As the years passed and the English siege of Orléans tightened, the voices became urgent and specific: Joan must leave her village, don male attire to protect her modesty among soldiers, ride to the Dauphin at Chinon, break the siege of Orléans, and lead Charles to be crowned with holy oil in the traditional coronation cathedral at Reims, deep behind English lines. Convinced that she was acting under divine mandate, the seventeen-year-old girl obeyed.  Joan of Arc's heavenly voices spoke to her in fluent French, comforting her in moments of isolation and urging her to trust in divine providence, assuring her that God had taken pity on the suffering kingdom of France and chosen her as His humble instrument.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RECOGNITION AT CHINON: MARCH 1429
Securing a small escort from the local royal captain Robert de Baudricourt at Vaucouleurs, Joan cut her hair short, dressed in male garments, and rode three hundred miles across dangerous, enemy-patrolled territory to the royal castle of Chinon. To test the peasant girl's claims, Charles VII staged a deliberate deception: he hid among the crowded courtiers in the grand hall, while a lavishly dressed nobleman sat upon the throne. Entering the chamber lit by fifty torches, Joan did not look at the fake king on the dais; instead, she walked directly through the crowd of three hundred courtiers and knelt before the simply dressed Charles, declaring: 'God give you life, gentle Dauphin. The King of Heaven sends me to you with a message that you shall be anointed and crowned in the city of Reims, and you shall be the lieutenant of the King of Heaven, who is the King of France.' Taking the Dauphin aside in private conversation, Joan revealed a secret known only to Charles and God, removing his deep doubts about his legitimate royal birth. Convinced of her authenticity after three weeks of rigorous interrogation by theologians at Poitiers, Charles granted her an army.  The private sign given by Joan to the Dauphin at Chinon was so profound that Charles VII's face reportedly turned radiant with joy, as the seventeen-year-old peasant girl confirmed his royal legitimacy, which had been cast into doubt by his own mother's scandalous court.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE WHITE BANNER OF ORLÉANS: MAY 1429
Equipped with a custom-fitted suit of gleaming white plate armor, a holy sword miraculously discovered buried behind the altar in the church of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, and a sacred white banner depicting Christ seated on clouds with two angels presenting lilies, Joan rode to the besieged city of Orléans at the head of a relief army. The city had been encircled for seven months by an imposing ring of English earthen and timber fortresses, called 'bastilles.' Joan immediately transformed the moral culture of the French army: she banned swearing, expelled prostitutes, and compelled the hardened mercenary soldiers to attend Mass and take confession. On April 29, 1429, Joan entered Orléans under cover of darkness to the ecstatic cheers of the starving citizens. Over the next nine days, Joan unleashed a whirlwind of aggressive offensive energy: on May 6, she led the assault on the fortress of Saint-Loup; on May 7, during the fierce assault on the heavily fortified bridgehead fortress of Les Tourelles, an English crossbow bolt pierced Joan's shoulder, passing through her armor. Weeping in physical pain, Joan pulled the arrow out with her own hands, returned to the front lines, raised her white banner, and rallied the French troops to storm the fortress. On May 8, the humiliated English army broke camp and retreated in disarray.  Joan's tactical presence at Orléans electrified French morale. Hardened veteran captains like Dunois and La Hire, who had previously known only retreat and defeat, marveled at the aggressive offensive confidence of the young girl who rode in the front lines with her sacred banner.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE CORONATION AT REIMS: JULY 1429
The lifting of the siege of Orléans was hailed across Europe as an undeniable divine miracle, shattering the aura of English military invincibility. Rather than consolidating positions, Joan urged Charles to embark immediately upon the perilous 'Coronation Campaign'—marching two hundred miles through the heart of English-held Champagne to the historic cathedral city of Reims. Sweeping through the Loire Valley, French forces crushed the veteran English army under Sir John Fastolf and Lord Talbot at the Battle of Patay, where French cavalry routed the feared English longbowmen before they could set up their protective wooden stakes. City after city—Troyes, Châlons, and Reims—opened their gates without firing a shot. On Sunday, July 17, 1429, inside the magnificent Gothic cathedral of Notre-Dame de Reims, Charles VII was anointed with the sacred holy oil of Clovis and crowned King of France. Standing beside the high altar, holding her sacred white banner, Joan wept with joy, declaring: 'Gentle King, now is fulfilled the pleasure of God, who willed that you should come to Reims to receive your coronation, showing that you are the true king, and he to whom the kingdom of France belongs.'  The march to Reims was an astonishing psychological triumph: English garrisons abandoned their fortresses without resistance, and rebellious towns opened their gates, as the French populace flocked to touch Joan's horse and kiss the hem of her garments in reverent joy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: BETRAYAL AT COMPIÈGNE AND THE TRIAL AT ROUEN
Following the coronation, royal counselors around Charles VII, jealous of Joan's influence and eager for diplomatic compromises with Burgundy, undermined her offensive campaigns. An assault on Paris failed, and Joan was wounded in the thigh. In May 1430, while defending the besieged town of Compiègne against Burgundian forces, Joan stayed in the rear guard to protect her retreating soldiers. The town gates were prematurely closed, and Joan was dragged from her horse and captured. Sold by the Duke of Burgundy to the English for the immense sum of ten thousand gold crowns, Joan was imprisoned in an iron cage in the castle of Rouen. Charles VII did not offer a single livre for her ransom. Determined to prove that Charles's coronation was the work of a witch, the English orchestrated a corrupt ecclesiastical trial led by Pierre Cauchon, the pro-English Bishop of Beauvais. For five grueling months, the nineteen-year-old illiterate girl faced sixty hostile theologians and inquisitors without legal counsel, astonishing her interrogators with sharp, inspired answers. When asked if she knew she was in God's grace, Joan deftly avoided the theological trap: 'If I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God so keep me.'  The transcripts of Joan's trial at Rouen, recorded verbatim in Latin by royal clerks and preserved today in French national archives, reveal her unmatched poise, sharp theological wit, and steadfast refusal to betray her heavenly voices despite continuous psychological torment.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE STAKE AT THE OLD MARKET: MAY 30, 1431
Condemned on seventy false charges of heresy, witchcraft, and the 'abomination' of wearing male clothing, Joan was sentenced to death. On the morning of May 30, 1431, in the Old Market square of Rouen, nineteen-year-old Joan was bound to a tall plaster stake surrounded by firewood, wearing a paper mitre inscribed with the words 'Heretic, Relapsed, Apostate, Idolater.' She asked an English soldier for a cross; he tied two sticks together, and she kissed it and placed it in her bodice. A Dominican friar held a church crucifix high before her face as the executioner lit the pyre. As the flames engulfed her body, Joan repeatedly cried out the sacred name of 'Jesus!' with her dying breath. Watching the execution, an English royal secretary named John Tressart wept in horror, crying aloud: 'We are lost; we have burned a saint!' Her heart miraculously remained unconsumed by the fire; the English ordered her ashes thrown into the Seine River to prevent her relics from being venerated. Twenty-five years later, a papal Rehabilitation Trial declared Joan innocent of all charges, clearing her name. Canonized as a saint in 1920, the peasant girl of Domremy stands as the eternal soul of France, whose courage turned the tide of history.  Joan of Arc's execution shocked even her English captors, who witnessed her dying cries of faith. Today, a tall modern cross marks the site of the stake in the Old Market of Rouen, where the peasant girl who saved France gave her life for her nation and her God.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Joan of Arc's sacrifice birthed a unified, sovereign France from the ashes of medieval war. Two centuries later, that French monarchy would reach the absolute pinnacle of absolute power and artistic magnificence under a single, all-powerful ruler. Next week, we continue our French saga with Episode 215: The Sun King: Louis XIV, the Hall of Mirrors, and the Man in the Iron Mask: the boy who fled the Fronde, the transformation of a swamp into the Palace of Versailles, the golden etiquette of the court, and the dark mystery of the masked prisoner. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
